text: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition
section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition

text: Zijie Mao 1, Xianglong Du 2, Xindi Xu 1, Yicai Wu 1, Xiaohui Yang 2* Kun Jiang 1, Jun Cheng 2, Zhi-You Zhou 2, Shi-Gang Sun 2 & Wen-Bin Cai.1* Received January 7, 2025; accepted March 9, 2025; published online May 6, 2025 Cobalt (Co) metallization presents a promising alternative strategy for the bottom interconnect in advanced chip manufacture, yet the interfacial structure and functionality ofan organic additive essential for superconformal Co deposition is far from clear given the concurring hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Herein, interfacial electrochemistry for a model additive molecule MBIS (sodium 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonate) at a Co electrode is investigated by applying in situ surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy and electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance combined with density functional theory calculations The vertical plane adsorption of MBIS on the Co surface via thiolate reduces the overall reduction current with a higher/lower Faradaic efficiency (FE) towards HER/Co deposition due to the significant blockage of surface Co sites as well as the formation of Co(II) complex with MBIS.

text: Surface coverage of MBIS is found to decrease with increasing pH and overpotential, which may account for the location-dependent functionality of MBIS in practical Co deposition in vias. This work provides a molecularlevel insight into the interfacial mechanism of an organic additive essential for the Co superfilling scenario.

text: 1 Introduction
section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 1 Introduction

text: The interconnect metallization is crucial to attain signal and electrical transmission and thus a central process in chip manufacturing [1–5]. Cu is the most commonly used interconnect metal by means of Damascene Cu plating, however, when a 14-nm (or below) process is adopted, electron scattering at external surfaces and grain boundaries leads to a sharp rise in the resistance of narrow Cu lines in the bottom layers [6]. At the nanoscale, the resistivity of a metal is directly related to ρ _b × λ, where ρ _b represents the bulk resistivity of the metal and λ represents the electron mean free path [7,8]. Co, Ru, Rh, and Mo have lower ρ _b × λ values and thus are expected to exhibit lower resistances in narrow lines. In addition, their higher melting points compared to that of Cu, are also beneficial in reducing electromigration [9]. In particular, Co interconnect by electrodeposition is highly promising for commercial applications because of its low cost and relative ease for plating among the four alternative metals [10,11].
section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 1 Introduction

text: Unlike acidic Cu electroplating in which hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is negligible, Co electroplating is accompanied by HER given that φ _Co ^2 + / Co = - 0.2 8 : V vs. SHE and φ_H^+/H_2=0 : V vs. SHE [12,13]. In order to achieve bottom-up filling and avoid voids in the vias, a suitable inhibiting additive, such as sodium 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonate (MBIS) [14], or dimethylglyoxime among others [15–25], is needed to regulate the kinetics of Co deposition. Several superfilling (superconformal deposition) models have been proposed to account for the additive-assisted filling process, including the S-shaped negative differential resistance (S-NDR) [15,26,27], the differential current efficiency fill (DCEF) model [28,29], and the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation (HID) model [30,31].
section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 1 Introduction

text: Notably, despite their significant achievement from a simulation perspective, these models lack a molecular-level insight into the interaction of a specific organic additive with a Co electrode as well as its impact on the Co electrodeposition, which is otherwise highly demanded for the mechanistic understanding and design ofadvanced additives. Along this line, in situ surface molecular spectroscopies are expected to be valuable for this purpose. The use of surface Raman spectroscopy is limited owing to the very low SERS activity at Co surfaces and the very difficult optical focusing with the strong HER condition. This challenge can be well addressed by the application of the in situ ATR-SEIRAS technique which is least metal-specific and free of gas evolution concern [32–40]. Besides, the convincing analysis of ATR-SEIRAS results towards the assignment of vibrational peaks and the determination of adsorption geometries calls for supplemental support of relevant density functional theory (DFT) calculations.
section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 1 Introduction

text: In this work, MBIS, an organic additive already validated for nano-vias Co superfilling [14], is selected as the target model molecule. The interfacial structure and mechanistic aspect of adsorbed MBIS at the Co electrode are probed initially by high sensitivity in situ ATR-SEIRAS and DFT calculations. Electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM) is applied to quantify the relative contributions of Co deposition and HER in the Co-plating solutions with and without the additive. Potential and pH dependencies of MBIS on Co deposition rates provide an inference to the interfacial functionality of MBIS in Co superfilling.

text: Figure 1a illustrates the linear sweep voltammograms (LSVs) for Co electrodes in 0.5 MH_3 BO _3 + 0.0 5 M CoSO_4 solutions with and without 25 ppm MBIS at pHs 2 and 3. In the absence of MBIS, the current density increases with the negative potential scan, owing to hydrogen evolution and Co deposition. Lowering the pH from 3 (black line) to 2 (red line) increases the current density at potentials negative of −1.55 V. In the presence of MBIS, the overall reduction current is strongly inhibited from −1.20 to −1.45 V, followed by a sharp increase regardless of pH, which was attributed to the inactivation of the additive [14]. At more negative potentials, the reduction currents largely overlap regardless of MBIS in the solution for a given pH. The closeness of the inactivation potentials for the two pHs suggests that the inactivation process is not H ^+ dependent.

text: Given the two reduction reactions involved, EQCM was utilized to evaluate the Faradaic efficiencies and thus the partial current densities for Co deposition and HER at varying pHs and potentials, as depicted in Figure 1b. The evaluation of FE _Co through the EQCM measurement is explained in Figure S1 (Supporting Information online). In the MBIS-free solution of pH 3, the FE _Co increases from 68% to 90% as the potential moves from −1.3 to −1.7 V since a more negative potential favors the more difficultly reduced Co ^2 + At a given potential, FE _H_2 increases upon decreasing the solution acidity to pH 2 (red lines).

text: In an MBIS-containing electrolyte, FE _Co is significantly decreased at potentials positive of −1.4 V, as compared to the counterpart in the MBIS-free electrolyte. Increasing the overpotential narrows the difference between Co deposition Faradaic efficiencies with and without MBIS. Notably, a steep rise of FE _Co from −1.5 to −1.6 V occurs due to the inactivation of MBIS as shown in Figure 1a. In fact, FE _Co is almost unchanged at −1.7 V for a given pH regardless of MBIS in a plating solution. Therefore, it may be concluded that the MBIS functions to decrease the Co deposition rate more than the HER rate, leading to a higher FE _H_2 and a lower FE _Co in an MBIS-contained plating solution. To gain a deeper mechanistic understanding, in situ ATR-SEIRAS was employed to study the adsorption behavior of MBIS on a Co film electrode which was pre-characterized by atomic force microscope (AFM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Figures S2 and S3).

text: Figure 2a displays the timeevolved ATR-SEIRAS spectra for MBIS adsorption at the Co electrode at −1.0 V in a 0.5 MH _3 BO _3 and 0.0 5 MNa _2 SO _4 solution containing 25 ppm MBIS, and the infrared (IR) spectra for solid MBIS and 30 g/L MBIS solution are shown in Figure S4 for comparison. Na _2 SO _4 was used as the supporting electrolyte instead of CoSO_4 in the solution to avoid the fluctuating spectral response due to otherwise the fast growth of the Co film, to ensure the acquisition of highquality IR spectra for MBIS adsorption on Co surfaces. It can be seen in Figure 2a, that MBIS adsorbed rapidly at the Co electrode and the peaks between 1520 to 7 3 1 ~ cm ^- 1 are assigned in Table S1 (Supporting Information online), corresponding to the vibrations of the functional groups of adsorbed MBIS. Strictly speaking, the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom of N-3 in the imidazole molecule is protonated for the pHs herein, for simplification, MBIS is also used to represent its protonated form in this work.

text: The adsorption structure of MBIS on the Co electrode was further confirmed. The vibrational frequencies and intensities of MBIS were calculated using DFT based on harmonic approximation, and the results are displayed in Figure S5 and MOV 1 (see the details in Supporting Information online). By comparing the infrared spectra of adsorbed MBIS with that of an MBIS solution (black line in Figure 2a), the adsorption configuration of MBIS at the Co electrode surface can be calculated by the surface selection rule of ATR-SEIRAS (see Figure S6 for more details). Thus, the MBIS molecule is deduced to adsorb nearly perpendicularly on the Co electrode via thiolate formation, i.e., at an angle of5° between the molecular plane and the local surface normal (defined as α), while the quasi-symmetric axis of the aromatic ring is edge-tilted by ca. 5° from the surface normal (defined as β).. To validate the adsorption configuration of MBIS on the Co surface, the structure optimization of adsorbed MBIS was also performed by DFT calculations as shown in Figure 2b, revealing that the corresponding angles α and β are both 4 ^°..

text: The consistent results from both approaches indicate that MBIS molecules are adsorbed in an essentially vertical orientation on the Co surface. Such an adsorption configuration enables a relatively high coverage of MBIS on the Co electrode surface, leading to a strong inhibition effect.

text: High sensitivity in situ ATR-SEIRAS measurement was extended to elucidate how the interfacial molecular structure affects the observed functionality of adsorbed MBIS towards Co electrodeposition, that is, inhibition on both partial currents with a lower FE _ Co and a higher FE _ H _ 2. On one hand, Figure 3a shows the ν(O‒H) spectral region for interfacial H _ 2 O at the Co electrode after introducing MBIS molecules in the solution. The broad wavy bipolar band in Figure 3a can be deconvoluted into four ν(O‒H) peaks due to four types of interfacial water, i. e., ice-like H _ 2 O \ ( ~ 3 3 0 0 \ cm ^ - 1), peak 1), bulk-like H _ 2 O \ ( ~ 3 4 2 0 \ cm ^ - 1, peak 2), hydrogen-bond partially broken H _ 2 O ( ~ 3 5 5 0 \ cm ^ - 1), peak 3) and hydrogen-bond broken H _ 2 O \ ( ~ 3 6 3 0 \ cm ^ - 1), peak 4) [41], noting that the ν(O‒H) vibration frequency of interfacial water increases with decreasing hydrogen bonding. The deconvolution results for the first and last curves in Figure 3a are shown in Figure 3b.

text: The vibrational peaks of the adsorbed MBIS corresponding to the C=C of aromatic ring stretching modes such as the peaks at 1512 and 1465~cm^-1 are redshifted significantly with Co ^2 + addition (indicated by the arrows in Figure 4b), suggesting a decrease in the π-conjugate-electron density of adsorbed MBIS due to its partial electron transfer to adjacent Co ^2 + to form a sort of Co(II)-MBIS complex. Besides the reduced surface active sites, this latter species is more difficult to reduce than hydrated Co ^2 + ions, leading to the overall inhibited Co deposition with a lower partial current and a Faradaic efficiency for Co deposition. DFT calculations also indicate that the approaching of Co ^2 + to MBIS results in an overall redshift in the vibrational frequencies, see Figure _4c and MOV 2 in the Supporting Information online. Note that the calculated spectra were performed for an MBIS solution, the relative peak positions and intensities are somewhat different from those experimentally observed in the ATR-SEIRAS spectra, nevertheless, the redshift trend matches.

The main peak at 1 0 3 3 ~ cm ^- 1 (marked with a star in Figure 5) for adsorbed MBIS increases by ~10% with pH decreased from 3 to ^2, consistent with a more significant reduction of FE _Co at pH 2 than at pH 3 as shown in Figure 1. text: During cathodic scanning, no additional spectral features characteristic of other new species can be seen except that the peak intensities for adsorbed MBIS tend to decrease, as a result of the MBIS desorption from the Co electrode. Reversing the potential scan results in the increment of the peak intensities. The normalized 1 0 3 3 ~ cm ^- 1 peak (marked with a star in Figure 6a) intensities versus potential plot (red solid line) for the negative potential scan is shown in Figure 6b using the one at −1.0 V as a benchmark. Obviously, the relative spectral coverage θ decreases with decreasing potential, specifically at −1.6 V, the θ value is only 8% of that at −1.0 V, implying that the deactivation of MBIS at the Co electrode is not due to the structural destruction of MBIS, but rather to potential-driven MBIS desorption. We believe that the low coverage of MBIS may at least partly account for similar electrochemical responses observed at very negative potentials in Figure 1.

text: Figure 6b (black dashed line) also displays a potential dependency of less than 10cm^-1/V for the 1 0 3 3 ~ cm ^- 1 peak (marked with a star in Figure 6a). It is noteworthy that the trend of the peak frequency follows that of θ as a function of potential, suggesting a strong correlation between the two plots. In fact, such a coincidence is also found for other ring vibration modes. The progressive desorption of MBIS with negatively moving potential leads to a weakening of the dipole-dipole interaction among adsorbed MBIS molecules, and thus a small displacement of the vibrational frequencies. In fact, given that the aromatic ring structure of vertically adsorbed MBIS molecules is barely affected by the electric field of the Helmholtz layer, the relevant Stark effect shall be very weak.

text: To further investigate the mechanism, the molecular dynamics simulations were performed using classical force fields (see the details in Supporting Information online). Based on the aforementioned results and molecular dynamics simulations, the interfacial mechanism of MBIS on Co electrodes may be proposed (Figure 7). The hydrophobicity of MBIS aromatic rings disrupts the hydrogen bonding of interfacial H_2 O,, leading to the formation of a more ordered H_2O structure in favor of HER (1 of the left panel of Figure 7). The positively charged Co ^2 + ions are driven towards the electrode surface by the electric field, forming an interfacial Co(II)-MBIS complex that requires higher energy input for its reduction (2, 3 of left panel of Figure 7). On one hand, the adsorption of MBIS reduces the number of surface active sites and decreases the apparent overall current. On the other hand, the formation of a Co(II) complex at the MBIS-modified Co electrode inhibit the Co deposition much more significantly than the HER, leading to a decrease in FE _Co and an increase in FE _H _2..

text: As a proven additive in the Co superfilling, MBIS essentially displays the feature of a strong inhibitor against Co deposition. The inhibition effect of MBIS is highly dependent on its surface coverage: the higher the coverage, the stronger the inhibition against Co deposition. Thus, the mechanism of the Co superfilling in the vias could be qualitatively unraveled by assuming the existing difference of local surface MBIS coverage inside and outside the vias, which may arise from but not limited to the obstructed mass transport of MBIS and the pH difference caused by HER. The higher and lower MBIS coverages outside and inside the vias lead to slower and faster Co filling outside and inside the vias, respectively, ensuring the Co superfilling (right panel of Figure 7). Based on the above mechanistic understanding at the molecular level, we are constructing (will report in the near future) a simulation model of the Co filling process to quantitatively analyze the distribution of additives in the vias, as well as to predict the conditions for the Co superfilling.

text: 3 Conclusions
section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 3 Conclusions

text: In this study, we have delved into the inhibition mechanism of the additive MBIS in acidic Co electroplating using a synergistic approach inclusive of electrochemical and ATR-SEIRAS measurement as well as computational simulations.
section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 3 Conclusions

text: The MBIS molecule adapts a nearly vertical adsorption configuration on the Co electrode via the formation of thiolate, reducing both partial currents for Co deposition and H _ 2 evolution with a higher FE _ Co and a lower FE _ H _ 2,, as compared to the MBIS-free case. We have revealed at a molecular level that the adsorbed MBIS molecules disrupt the hydrogen bonding of interfacial water, and form a sort of interfacial MBIS-Co ^ 2 + complex, thereby favoring a higher selectivity toward the hydrogen evolution than the Co deposition. Furthermore, variation in the MBIS coverage has been identified with varying pHs or potentials, offering crucial insights into the refinement of electroplating parameters. The MBIS coverage-dependent inhibition effect can qualitatively account for the Co superfilling process. Our work is valuable in understanding the interfacial structure and functionality of a typical inhibitor for superconformal Co plating and lends important guidance for filling simulations.
